Hypothesis: the black powder is acting as a catalyst, providing an alternative pathway with a lower Ea.

Test: recover, dry and reweigh the powder after the reaction. A catalyst's mass is unchanged and no new products form. Any other valid hypothesis with a matching test is accepted.

Experiments 1 and 2: [S2O32−] constant, [H+] halved, rate unchanged → zero order in H+.
Experiments 2 and 3: [H+] constant, [S2O32−] halved, rate halved → first order in S2O32−.
rate = k[S2O32−] (H+ does not appear because it is zero order).
k = rate/[S2O32−] = 0.036/0.200 = 0.18; units s−1 (first-order overall: mol dm−3 s−1 ÷ mol dm−3).
S2O32− → S + SO32−. The rate-determining step must involve one S2O32− and no H+; any balanced (atoms and charge) equation starting from a single S2O32− is accepted.

Any three:

  • measure the rate at several different temperatures, keeping concentrations constant;
  • calculate k at each temperature;
  • plot ln k against 1/T;
  • gradient = −Ea/R, so Ea = −gradient × R.

Why: Arrhenius equation ln k = −Ea/RT + ln A is a straight line in ln k vs 1/T.

(i) HCl 10.0 cm3, Na2S2O3 20.0 cm3, water 20.0 cm3 – total volume stays 50.0 cm3 so only [S2O32−] halves.

(ii) So that the depth of liquid (thickness the mark is viewed through) stays the same – a fair test.

(iii) First order: rate halves, so the time doubles: 94 s.

(i) The slow step involves HS2O3− (formed from S2O32− + H+) and H+, so rate = k[S2O32−][H+]2.

(ii) Plot rate (= 1/time, s−1) against [HCl]: 0.0112, 0.0137, 0.0161, 0.0185 s−1 at 0.02, 0.04, 0.06, 0.08 mol dm−3. Marks: suitable labelled y-axis scale/units; rates correctly calculated; points plotted and joined with a line.

(iii) The graph is a straight line (linear dependence – doubling [HCl] does not quadruple the rate, so not second order in H+), and it does not pass through the origin.

(i) Axes: y = number (fraction) of particles, x = kinetic energy. Both curves start at the origin, are asymmetric and approach the x-axis without touching it. The T2 curve is broader, with a lower peak shifted to the right; same area. Ea marked on the energy axis.

(ii) Particles have more kinetic energy; collisions are more frequent (more collisions per unit time); and, most importantly, a much greater proportion of particles have energy ≥ Ea, so more collisions are successful.

(i) Draw a tangent to the curve at t = 0 and calculate its gradient.

(ii) The rate decreases with time, because the concentration of H2O2 (molecules per unit volume) decreases, so collisions become less frequent (fewer per second). 'Fewer collisions' without frequency does not score.

Axes: y = number/fraction of particles (probability); x = kinetic energy. Mark Ea(catalysed) to the left of Ea(uncatalysed). The catalyst provides an alternative pathway with lower Ea, so a greater proportion of molecules (shaded area) have energy ≥ Ea and more collisions are successful.

(i) The reactant is not involved in (or before) the rate-determining step (zero order), or it is in large excess.

(ii) rate = k[A] (zero order in B; stoichiometric coefficients are not orders).
A curve with positive slope that curves upwards (k rises exponentially with T, Arrhenius).
The change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time. Mass, amount or volume are accepted instead of concentration; 'substance' is not.

Any three:

  • particles must collide; rate depends on collision frequency
  • colliding particles must have energy ≥ the activation energy (Ea). This point must be included.
  • they must collide with the correct orientation (geometry)

(i) Experiments 1→2: halving [NaOH] halves the rate, so it is first order in NaOH. Experiments 1→4: halving [C₄H₉Br] halves the rate, so it is first order in C₄H₉Br.
Rate = k[OH⁻][C₄H₉Br]

(ii) k = 1.02 × 10⁻⁴ ÷ (0.25 × 0.25) = 1.6 × 10⁻³ mol⁻¹ dm³ s⁻¹

(iii) Bimolecular: two species collide in the rate-determining step (SN2).
The change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time. Mass, amount or volume are accepted; 'substance' is not.
Larger particles have a smaller surface area exposed to the other reactant, so the frequency of collisions (collisions per unit time) decreases.

(i) Step 2 (X + NO → Y + H₂O), the slow step.

(ii) The hypothesis is invalid. Only one H₂ is involved up to and including the slow step (in step 1, which forms X), so the reaction is first order in H₂: rate = k[NO]²[H₂]. The second mark is only awarded if the first is correct.

The rate increases. The catalyst provides an alternative pathway with a lower Ea, so a greater proportion of particles have enough energy and there are more successful collisions per unit time. 'Lowers Ea' alone is not enough.

The Arrhenius plot gives ln k = −Ea/(RT) + ln A, so the gradient = −Ea/R.

From the line, gradient ≈ −0.74 ÷ 0.0006 ≈ −1233 K (1200–1260 accepted).

Ea = 1233 × 8.31 = 1.02 × 10⁴ J mol⁻¹ = 10.2 kJ mol⁻¹ (3 s.f., with units).

(i) Experiments 1→2: [O₂] doubles and the rate doubles, so it is first order in O₂. Experiments 2→3: [NO] and [O₂] both double and the rate rises ×8; O₂ accounts for ×2, so NO gives ×4 and it is second order in NO.

(ii) rate = k[NO]²[O₂]

(iii) k = 1.05 × 10⁻³ ÷ ((2.30 × 10⁻²)² × 1.15 × 10⁻²) = 173 mol⁻² dm⁶ s⁻¹

(iv) Example: NO + NO ⇌ N₂O₂ (fast), then N₂O₂ + O₂ → 2NO₂ (slow, rate-determining). The species up to and including the slow step are 2NO + O₂, matching the rate expression. Alternatives such as NO + O₂ ⇌ NO₃ (fast) followed by NO₃ + NO → 2NO₂ (slow) are also accepted.

(i) 2NO(g) + 2H2(g) → N2(g) + 2H2O(g) (add the steps, cancel intermediates).

(ii) rate = k[NO]2[H2] – the slow step involves N2O2 (formed from 2NO) and H2.

(iii) Vary each concentration in turn, keeping the other constant, and measure the initial rate. Expect: doubling [NO] quadruples the rate (second order); doubling [H2] doubles the rate (first order).

(iv) No – different mechanisms can give the same rate expression; kinetics can only show consistency (or disprove).

(v) Measure the change in pressure with time at constant volume and temperature (4 mol gas → 3 mol gas), or volume change at constant pressure.

(i) Exothermic profile: products well below reactants; ΔH = −664 kJ arrow from reactants down to products; Ea = 63 kJ arrow from reactants up to the peak.

(ii) Dotted curve with a lower peak, same reactant and product levels, labelled “Catalysed”.

(iii) Higher-T curve: peak lower and shifted right, broader, with a longer tail (same area).

(iv) A greater proportion of particles have E ≥ Ea (more area under the curve beyond Ea); and particles move faster, so there is a greater frequency of collisions (not just “more collisions”).

Plot the five points (1/t × 10−3 against concentration): (0.030, 9.0), (0.060, 16.7), (0.090, 27.8), (0.120, 37.0), (0.150, 43.5).

Draw a straight best-fit line with a ruler, through the origin (gradient ≈ 300). Use a single line – do not join the points dot to dot.

(i) First order in thiosulfate: the rate (1/t) is directly proportional to [Na2S2O3] (straight line through the origin). “Linear” alone is not enough.

(ii) rate = k[Na2S2O3][HCl] (second order overall).

From the line at 0.075 mol dm−3: 1/t ≈ 22.5 × 10−3 s−1.

t = 1/(22.5 × 10−3) ≈ 44 s (42.4–46.4 s accepted). Do not average the times of neighbouring experiments, because t is not linear in concentration.

(i) Axes: y = number/fraction of particles, x = kinetic energy. The T2 curve has a lower peak, shifted right and a broader spread; both curves start at the origin.

(ii) A greater proportion of particles have E ≥ Ea (greater area beyond Ea), and faster particles give a greater frequency of collisions. The first point is the main reason.

At higher temperatures the reaction time is shorter, so the error in timing and in judging when the mark disappears is a larger percentage of the time. (The mixture may also cool during the reaction.)

(i) Use a colorimeter to follow the fading of the iodine colour over time (or take samples, quench them and titrate with thiosulfate). The method must measure a change over time.

(ii) Draw a best-fit straight line through the points. Gradient = Δ[I2]/Δt = (0.43 − 0.80)/50 → relative rate = 7.4 × 10−3 mol dm−3 s−1 (0.0070–0.0080 accepted). The rate is the magnitude of the negative gradient.

Relationship: when [H+] doubles, the rate doubles, so the rate is directly proportional to [H+] (0.05 → 0.0025, 0.10 → 0.0051, 0.20 → 0.0100).

Order with respect to H+: first.
Zero order in iodine. Reason: the lines for all three iodine concentrations have the same gradient (parallel straight lines), so the rate does not depend on [I2].

From A the line starts almost flat: with no catalyst the reaction is slow at first. The rate then gradually increases (the line gets steeper) because the reaction produces H+ ions, which catalyse it. This is called autocatalysis.

(i) The concentration of acid decreases as it is used up, so collisions become less frequent.

(ii) The curve starts at the origin with a steeper initial gradient (powder has a larger surface area), and levels off at the same final volume (same amount of acid, which is limiting).

(i) rate = k[NO2]2.

(ii) Step I is rate-determining: it involves two NO2 molecules, matching the rate equation, and CO (which appears only in step II) is not in the rate equation.

(iii) Follow the colour change over time by colorimetry or UV-vis/IR spectroscopy (NO2 is brown).

(iv) Ea(reverse) = Ea(forward) + |ΔH| = 132 + 226 = 358 kJ.

(v) An upward-curving (parabolic) line through the origin, because rate ∝ [NO2]2.
Activation energy is independent of temperature (it does not change). Temperature changes k through the e−Ea/RT term, i.e. the fraction of collisions with E ≥ Ea.

(i) The curve is steepest at the start because the concentration/number of reactant particles is greatest, so collisions are most frequent. As the reactants are used up, their concentration falls, collision frequency decreases and the gradient (rate) decreases until it levels off.
Key idea: rate depends on the frequency of collisions.

(ii) More gas is produced in X, so more reactant was present: a greater mass/amount of metal carbonate in X or a greater concentration/amount of ethanoic acid in X (whichever is limiting).

(i) Cl2: Exp 1→2, [Cl2] doubles, rate doubles → first order.
NO: Exp 2→3, [NO] doubles, rate × 4 (0.790 → 3.16) → second order.

(ii) rate = k[NO]2[Cl2]

(iii) From Exp 1: k = 0.395 ÷ (0.1302 × 0.130) = 180 dm6 mol−2 min−1 (1.80 × 102).

Any two:
• loss of mass (CO2 escapes)
• volume of CO2 gas produced
• change in pH (HCl used up)
• change in conductivity
• change in temperature

(i) Any one: at high concentration the reaction is very fast and hard to measure accurately; so many CO2 bubbles form that they reduce contact between acid and CaCO3; CaCO3 becomes the limiting reagent (HCl in excess).

(ii) A straight line through the origin passing as close as possible to A, B and C.

(iii) Rate is directly proportional to [HCl] (first order).

(iv) rate = k[HCl] (or k[H+])

(v) k = gradient = rate/[HCl], e.g. 9 × 10−3 ÷ 0.45 ≈ 0.02 s−1 (units of a first-order rate constant: s−1).
Read off (or extrapolate) the best-fit line at 1.00 mol dm−3: rate ≈ 20.5 × 10−3 mol dm−3 s−1 (19.5–21.5 × 10−3), i.e. k × 1.00.

Method 1: Carry out the reaction at several temperatures and find k at each. Plot ln k against 1/T. The gradient = −Ea/R, so Ea = −gradient × R.

Method 2: Measure the rate constants at two temperatures and use ln(k1/k2) = (Ea/R)(1/T2 − 1/T1).

• Axes labelled: y = number/fraction of particles (with that energy); x = (kinetic) energy.
• Curve starts at the origin, rises to a peak, then tails off towards (but never touches) the x-axis; skewed to the right.
• Mark both activation energies on the x-axis with Ea(catalyst) < Ea(uncatalysed).

Why: with a catalyst a greater area (more particles) lies beyond Ea.

(i) A curve starting at the origin with a steeper initial gradient, levelling off at the same final volume (same mass of CaCO3; acid in excess). Crushing increases surface area, not the amount.

(ii) The rate decreases, because ethanoic acid is a weak acid, only partially dissociated, so [H+] is lower and there are fewer successful collisions per second.

(i) [N2O2] decreases – the forward reaction is exothermic, so increasing T favours the reverse (endothermic) reaction.

(ii) Rate is set by the slow step: rate = k2[N2O2][O2].
N2O2 is an intermediate; from the fast equilibrium, [N2O2] = Kc[NO]2.
Substituting: rate = k[NO]2[O2] (k = k2Kc).

T1 = 298 K, T2 = 308 K, k2/k1 = 2.
ln(k2/k1) = (Ea/R)(1/T1 − 1/T2)
ln 2 = (Ea/8.31)(1/298 − 1/308) → 0.693 = (Ea/8.31)(1.09 × 10−4)
Ea ≈ 5.29 × 104 J mol−1 = 52.9 kJ mol−1

(i) Curve starts at the origin ([FeSO4] = 0), rises, and its gradient decreases steadily until it levels off (reactant being used up).

(ii) Draw a tangent to the curve at t = 0; the initial rate equals the gradient of that tangent.

(iii) A single piece has a smaller surface area, so fewer Cu2+ ions can collide with iron at any moment → lower frequency of collisions (fewer collisions per second), so slower rate. (“Fewer collisions” alone, without per unit time, is not enough.)

B: reactant – it is used up in both steps and is not regenerated.

D: intermediate – it is made in step 1 and used up in step 2.

(A is the catalyst: used in step 1, regenerated in step 2.)
rate = k[A][B] – the rate equation follows the slow (rate-determining) step, A + B → C + D.
The reaction is first order in A; [A] increases ×1.5 with [B] constant, so rate increases ×1.5: 1.20 × 1.5 = 1.80 mol dm−3 s−1.
Hydrogen peroxide (like many chemicals) decomposes in light; brown glass blocks light (UV/visible) and slows this.

(i) Plot the four points; draw a straight best-fit line through the origin. Rate = gradient ≈ 15.0 cm3 ÷ 700 s = 0.022 cm3 O2 s−1 (0.020–0.024).

(ii) Trial 2 doubles [H2O2] (KI same, total volume same) → rate doubles (0.022 → 0.043): first order in H2O2. Trial 3 doubles [KI] → rate doubles: first order in KI. Rate = k[H2O2][KI]; overall order 2.

(iii) Both curves start at the origin; the T2 curve has its peak lower and to the right of T1, and its tail lies above T1 at high energies (same area under both).

(iv) Mark Ea on the energy axis. At T2, the area under the curve beyond Ea is greater, so a larger proportion of particles have E ≥ Ea → more successful collisions.

(v) Manganese(IV) oxide (manganese dioxide).
Rate decreases: at lower pressure there are fewer molecules per unit volume (lower concentration), so the collision frequency (collisions per unit time) is lower.

(i) At t = 2 about half the N2O has gone (the graph shows half the pressure rise), so [N2O] has halved and, as the reaction is first order, the rate is half the initial rate.

(ii) If step 1 is the slow, rate-determining step, the rate depends only on it; step 1 is unimolecular (one N2O molecule), so rate = k[N2O] – first order, as observed. (If step 2 were slow, the rate would also depend on [O].)
The new curve has a smaller initial gradient (slower reaction), and, since p ∝ T at fixed V and n, the initial and final pressures are both lower by a similar factor.

Mark two activation energies on the energy axis, with Ea(catalysed) lower than Ea(uncatalysed). With the catalyst a greater proportion of molecules have E ≥ Ea (greater area under the curve to the right of Ea), so more collisions are successful per unit time.

(i) Exp 1→3: [OH−] constant, [C3H7Cl] triples and rate triples (3.1 → 9.2 × 10−4) → first order in C3H7Cl. Exp 1→2: both concentrations double and rate quadruples (×4.2), so after the ×2 from C3H7Cl the remaining ×2 is due to OH− → first order in OH−. Rate = k[C3H7Cl][OH−].

(ii) SN2 (bimolecular nucleophilic substitution).

(iii) Curly arrow from a lone pair on O of OH− to the C bonded to Cl (backside attack); curly arrow from the C–Cl bond to Cl; transition state in square brackets with partial bonds HO···C···Cl and an overall negative charge; products CH3CH(OH)CH3 + Cl−. (Arrow must start on O, not on H.)

(i) Cu+: [Ar]3d10 (1s22s22p63s23p63d10) — 4s electron lost first.

(ii) ΔH° = ΣΔHf(products) − ΣΔHf(reactants) = 2(−241.8) − 4(−92.3) = −483.6 + 369.2 = −114.4 kJ. ΔHf of O2 and Cl2 are zero; use H2O(g).

(iii) Maxwell–Boltzmann: Ea(cat) marked to the left of Ea. Energy profile: a lower hump from reactants, with Ea(cat) smaller than Ea (same reactant and product levels).

(iv) The catalyst provides an alternative pathway with lower activation energy, so a larger proportion of particles have E ≥ Ea(cat) and the frequency of successful collisions increases.

Br−: Exp 2→3, [Br−] doubles, rate doubles → first order.

Rate = k[BrO3−][Br−][H+]2.
